accroche: At 4.2 kelvins, the electrical resistance of mercury does not decrease gradually: it collapses all at once, until it becomes undetectable.
contenu_vulgarise:
On April 8, 1911, in his laboratory in Leiden, in the Netherlands, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes lowers the temperature of a mercury wire toward absolute zero and monitors its electrical resistance. He notes, in Dutch, in his laboratory notebook: “Kwik nagenoeg nul,” mercury practically zero. The resistance does not decrease little by little: it collapses, almost all at once.

## A Drop, Not a Slope

Three years earlier, on July 10, 1908, Kamerlingh Onnes had been the first to liquefy helium, opening access to temperatures never before reached in a laboratory. Studying how metals conduct electricity near absolute zero then becomes possible. He chooses mercury for two precise reasons: its resistance curve, measured at 14 kelvins, showed no sign of leveling off, unlike gold or platinum, and the Leiden laboratory had long mastered the purification of mercury by distillation, after which it is poured liquid into a fine tube, without the risk of contamination that drawing a metal wire involves.

The measurement of April 8, 1911 is refined in the following months. On October 26, a new experiment fixes the transition temperature at 4.20 kelvins, over an interval of less than a hundredth of a degree, a remarkable precision for the time. Kamerlingh Onnes puts it this way in his Nobel Prize lecture, in December 1913: “the mercury at 4.2°K has entered a new state, which, owing to its particular electrical properties, can be called the state of superconductivity.”

## No Sleeping Assistant, and Not Quite the Right Prize

A widespread anecdote has it that a young assistant fell asleep, letting the helium warm up, and that an accidental effect thus revealed the transition. Two Leiden researchers, reopening the original laboratory notebooks preserved at the Boerhaave museum, have shown that the measurement of May 23, 1911 was on the contrary carried out deliberately with rising temperature, step by step, precisely to refine control of the experiment. Nothing accidental there.

Another useful point: the 1913 Nobel Prize in Physics does not, to the letter, reward the discovery of superconductivity. Its official wording concerns his investigations on the properties of matter at low temperatures, which led in particular to the production of liquid helium. Superconductivity, discovered two years earlier, belongs to the same research program, but the Nobel committee mentioned it in passing, without making it the reason for the prize.

Since then, tin and lead have joined mercury on the list of metals that are superconducting at very low temperatures. The need for liquid helium, costly and difficult to maintain, has steered decades of research toward superconducting materials at less extreme temperatures, a quest still under way, more than a century after Kamerlingh Onnes's notebook.

repere.texte: On April 8, 1911, Kamerlingh Onnes's laboratory notebook bears a simple note in Dutch: “Kwik nagenoeg nul,” “mercury practically zero.” The precise measurement of the transition temperature, 4.20 kelvins over an interval of less than 0.01 kelvin, would be established only six months later, on October 26, 1911.
repere.source: Dirk van Delft & Peter Kes, “The Discovery of Superconductivity,” Physics Today, 2010, based on the original notebooks of the Boerhaave museum

carte.idee: On April 8, 1911, in Leiden, Kamerlingh Onnes sees the electrical resistance of mercury collapse all at once near absolute zero, rather than decrease gradually. He has just discovered superconductivity, a phenomenon that his 1913 Nobel Prize, however, does not officially reward.

quiz.question: Why does Kamerlingh Onnes choose mercury for his 1911 experiment, rather than gold or platinum?
choix: Mercury was the only metal liquid at room temperature available in the laboratory
Gold and platinum do not conduct electricity at all at low temperature
Mercury cost far less to buy than gold or platinum
Its resistance curve showed no leveling off, and Leiden knew how to purify it finely
quiz.explication: Neither its price nor its being liquid motivates the choice of mercury: its electrical resistance, measured at 14 kelvins, showed no sign of leveling off, and the Leiden laboratory knew how to purify it by distillation to an unmatched purity, avoiding the defects introduced by drawing a metal wire.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which widespread anecdote about the 1911 discovery did the original laboratory notebooks refute?
choix: That a sleeping assistant supposedly let the helium warm up by accident
That Kamerlingh Onnes supposedly stole the idea from a German colleague
That the first measurement was supposedly made with lead, not mercury
That the experiment supposedly failed three times before succeeding
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Two researchers showed, by reopening the notebooks of the Boerhaave museum, that the measurement of May 23, 1911 was carried out deliberately, with no sleeping assistant.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the 1913 Nobel Prize in Physics awarded to Kamerlingh Onnes officially reward, to the letter?
choix: The discovery of superconductivity itself, named explicitly
His investigations on the properties of matter at low temperatures
The invention of the first industrial superconducting wire
His collaboration with Albert Einstein on thermodynamics
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The official wording of the prize concerns his investigations on the properties of matter at low temperatures, without explicitly naming superconductivity.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what date and at what temperature is the transition of mercury precisely measured?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is a new experiment of October 26, 1911 that fixes the transition temperature at 4.20 kelvins, over an interval of less than a hundredth of a degree.
